g.text: Identify all 10 primary structures of a flowering plant.

svg.text: How pollen is transferred from anther to stigma — the first step of plant reproduction.

g.text: Cross-pollination transfers genetic material between flowers, producing
offspring with greater genetic diversity than self-pollination.
Ten label tiles — drag each to the matching drop zone above.
Use these clues to identify each part:
The center is the female reproductive column (pistil).
It has three sections: sticky top (stigma), narrow neck (style), and a swollen base (ovary).
Surrounding the pistil are the stamens (male parts).
Each stamen = filament (thin stalk) + anther (yellow pollen sac at the tip).
Petals attract pollinators; sepals (green, at the very base) protected the bud.
Look for the swollen green cup at the flower's base.
That is the receptacle — where every other floral part attaches.
Mnemonic: "Stigma Sits Sticky, Style Strings Straight."
Ovary is at the base — think "O" for "on the bottom."
Start with the parts you know — petals and sepals are usually the easiest.
Each numbered drop zone corresponds to one flower part. Compare with your answers:
Sticky top of pistil — receives pollen grains.
Yellow pollen-producing sac at the tip of the stamen.
Slender tube connecting stigma to ovary — pollen tube path.
The thin stalk that supports and lifts the anther.
Enlarged base of pistil — contains ovules (future seeds).
The whole male organ — filament plus anther together.
The complete female organ — stigma + style + ovary.
Green outermost part — protected the bud before it opened.
Thickened tip of stem — attachment point for all floral parts.
